# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review of Varga and Holm's comment on the Halden pilot

The first half of this comment is valuable. It uses the microdata to put numbers on problems the working paper glossed over, and the attrition finding is new and damaging to the pilot. But the conclusion goes well beyond what the analysis supports. The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by:
- the authors' own corrected estimate of +10.8%, which is still a gain;
- the Varden trial, which the comment cites selectively.

There are also an arithmetic inconsistency, a correction the abstract claims but never makes, and a mischaracterisation of the Varden meetings analysis.

## Arithmetic

Most figures check out:

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Table 2, as reported | 98.7 / 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Table 2, record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Table 2, manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Table 2, record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% |
| Hours, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 | ratio 0.859, a 14.1% fall |
| Hours, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 | ratio 0.861, a 13.9% fall |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% |

Two figures don't check out:

- **The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** The two sources of extra time are +0.7 hours per day over four days (2.8 hours) and 1.6 hours on the day off, 4.4 hours in total. Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours a week, not the 34.6 reported. The pieces would only fit if the daily increase were about +0.25 hours. Either a component is wrong or the actual-hours figure is. If actual hours were nearer 36.4, the per-hour gain would shrink further, so this matters for the authors' own argument.
- **The novelty extrapolation is off.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months three and six, a drop of 0.32 in three months. At that rate it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten."

A minor point: the exit forms account for only eight of the nine withdrawals (six workload, two scheduling).

## What holds up

- **Attrition.** Seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule had started, and most gave workload as the reason. This directly contradicts the working paper's account and is the comment's most important contribution.
- **Manager ratings vs records.** Managers' ratings exceeded the record-based index in 19 of 23 organisations, which is very unlikely by chance (sign test p ≈ 0.001). The bias is systematic.
- **Actual hours.** Using actual rather than scheduled hours, and deflating revenue for inflation, are both correct. They match the problems I flagged in the working paper, now with numbers attached.
- **Recommendations.** The recommendations for future evaluations are sound.

## Main problems

**1. The conclusion is contradicted by evidence the comment itself cites.**
- **Varden's case-processing stratum.** It addresses each problem the comment raises: it was randomised, used administrative output records and timesheet hours, and ran for nine months. It found output per FTE statistically unchanged and output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4). The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions the case-processing stratum from the same trial.
- **Varden's counter stratum.** Even there, output per actual hour rose by 6.7%.

The defensible conclusion is that per-hour gains are much smaller than uncontrolled pilots report and are not sector-general. "Entirely an artifact" is not defensible. Moving from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general makes the overreach worse.

**2. Attrition is never corrected, despite the abstract.** The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain down to 10.8%. But Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The 10.8% still comes from survivors. With exit data in hand, the authors could:
- include the withdrawn organisations under explicit assumptions (for example, output at baseline, or output at 80);
- or report bounds.

Either would give a real attrition-corrected figure. As written, the abstract describes an analysis that wasn't done.

**3. The rows of Table 2 cover different organisations.** The four rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. Differences between rows therefore mix the effect of each correction with differences in which organisations are included. The Data Note admits that the subsets are non-random, but the table still reads as a step-by-step series of corrections. The authors should run all four specifications on the 17-organisation subset. That would isolate the effect of each correction.

**4. The novelty argument is untested, and the data to test it are available.**
- **Wrong variable.** Self-reported energy is not output. A decline in energy doesn't show a decline in productivity.
- **Weak extrapolation.** Drawing a straight line through two points is not evidence that energy returns to baseline. It could just as easily level off. The extrapolation is also miscalculated, as noted above.
- **The direct test exists.** The pilot collected output indexes monthly, and 27 organisations have continuous time-tracking. The authors have the microdata, so they could check directly whether output per actual hour declines from month to month. They don't.
- **Burden of proof.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]" is a reasonable reason to withhold judgement. It is not a reason to conclude that the residual is zero.

**5. The section on meetings misrepresents the Varden paper and applies a double standard.**
- **What Varden claimed.** The Varden authors called the analysis exploratory and said seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism." They also registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up. The comment argues against a stronger claim than Varden made.
- **"Subgroup selected after results were known."** The seven offices are all of Varden's treated case-processing offices. Data collection was requested by managers in month six. The comment gives no evidence that the offices were chosen with the results in mind.
- **Double standard.** The comment's own novelty explanation is also post hoc and unregistered, and it rests on two survey time points. If the meetings hypothesis "should not be cited as a mechanism," neither should the novelty hypothesis.

**6. Some record-based measures may build in the hours cut.** One of the listed record types is "billable hours delivered." For professional services, that measures time, not output, and it falls almost automatically when hours are cut. If several of the 23 organisations used it, the record-based index is biased downward relative to real output. The authors should break down the manager-vs-record gap by type of record.

## Smaller points

- **Retail.** The retail and hospitality figure from records (−11.2%) rests on three organisations. It points the same way as Varden's counter stratum, but it is very imprecise.
- **Revenue.** CPI is a rough deflator for these sectors' revenue, and nine organisations did not report revenue. The real-terms correction is right in direction, but its size is uncertain.
- **Which organisations have records.** Organisations with time-tracking and submitted records may be weighted toward software and professional services. A sector breakdown of the subsets would show which way the subset bias runs.

## Overall

**What's supported:**
- the Halden pilot overstated per-hour gains roughly twofold;
- attrition was misreported;
- per-employee output falls in work that depends on staff being present.

**What isn't supported:**
- that the remaining gain is zero;
- that it is caused by novelty;
- that the conclusion generalises beyond this pilot.

To close that gap, the comment would need:
1. an analysis that includes the withdrawn organisations or bounds their effect;
2. all four specifications run on the same 17-organisation subset;
3. a month-by-month check of output per hour;
4. engagement with Varden's case-processing result.

Without those, "entirely an artifact" should become something like "substantially overstated; durability undemonstrated."
